narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 58.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. At 22.5, it sits far below the average of 37.2 among students who were accepted, signaling that the model saw this as a major risk for bar exam success.

Your undergraduate GPA came next in importance, but worked in the opposite direction. The 2.9 GPA pulled the prediction slightly toward passing. While below the 3.23 average of accepted students, it still provided a modest positive signal.

Your family income bracket of Middle was the third most influential factor and also nudged the outcome slightly toward passing. This is fairly typical—34.8% of accepted students come from middle-income families, so it was not a negative.

Taken together, the large negative impact of your LSAT score outweighed the modest positive effects from your GPA and family income, resulting in the rejection.

What you should do next is focus on improving your LSAT score through targeted preparation. A meaningful increase here would likely change the model’s prediction and open doors to admission. Consider retaking the test and reapplying once your score improves.
